1	# CHANGE-BRIEF — Assignment 7: animation
     2	
     3	Written by me (decisions, phase table, cycle spec, predictions); Claude Code organised my decisions into this form and drafted the predictions and short answers, which I went through and confirmed one by one. My working draft is in Chinese; this is the English version.
     4	
     5	## Shared facts
     6	
     7	- Character: my main-character model `xz.blend`, commissioned for this project and used with permission. Animation is keyed in a working copy, `xz_anim.blend`, in Blender and exported to Godot as a `.glb` (the imported 3D route).
     8	- Frame rate: 30 fps. Frames are numbered from 0; frame N is at N / 30 s.
     9	- I describe or pose each motion; Claude keys it in Blender.
    10	- Sprite clip: a small character head in the corner of the tablet OS taskbar (see "Clip: pixel head").
    11	- Which clip loops: the sprite clip (pixel head) loops; the one-handed tablet raise is the committing action.
    12	- Godot version: 4.7.2-stable. Godot 4 class and property names only.
    13	- Clips are resources: the imported rig clips live in the `.glb` (owned by the character scene); the head clip lives in the head scene's `AnimationPlayer`. No clip is built in code at runtime.
    14	
    15	## The two clips
    16	
    17	| | Pixel head (taskbar) | One-handed tablet raise |
    18	|---|---|---|
    19	| What it communicates | The tablet OS is on and idle; every time the player takes the tablet out, they see their own character | The character is taking the tablet out, and when the tablet actually becomes usable |
    20	| Why the player needs it | Two jobs (my decision): a moving head shows the tablet OS is running and not frozen (a status cue); and it shows whose tablet this is (every player has their own tablet; later, in co-op, one each) | Taking the tablet out costs time: while raising it you cannot walk or jump, and the screen only lights once the tablet is in hand (a gameplay trade-off) |
    21	| Object it plays on | A `Sprite2D` in the tablet OS taskbar (head scene in `computer_system/tablet_os/system/pixel_head/`) | The player character (the xz model's `Skeleton3D` in `humanoid.tscn`); `TabletDevice` hangs on the `tablet` bone and follows it |
    22	| Route | Sprite2D + an `AnimationPlayer` frame track (keys `frame`) | Imported 3D rig (keyed in Blender, exported as `.glb`) |
    23	| Why this route | Only 8 cells and one loop: one integer track is the most direct, and the read-back can check that the track points at `Sprite2D:frame`, its update mode and its frame range | The character is already a commissioned 3D model with a full skeleton and IK controllers; the fingers and arm have to fit the tablet, which only the Blender controllers make precise |
    24	| The one authority | The `AnimationPlayer` in the head scene, autoplaying and looping. It reads no game state | The character's `AnimationTree` (state machine). It reads `Humanoid.get_tablet_hold()` (`humanoid.gd`) and changes state when the hold state changes |
    25	| Cycle or committing action | Cycle | Committing action (phase table below) |
    26	
    27	## Clip: pixel head (sprite sheet, loops)
    28	
    29	### Task
    30	
    31	A looping character head in the corner of the tablet OS taskbar. Eight frames side by side in one sprite sheet; in Godot a `Sprite2D` (`hframes` = 8, `vframes` = 1) with an `AnimationPlayer` that keys `frame` in order, discrete updates, looping.
    32	
    33	### Design (2026-11-22)
    34	
    35	| Item | Content |
    36	|---|---|
    37	| Image source | Pixel art generated with Codex: `avatar-idle-front-sheet-4x2-56.png` (4 × 2, transparent, 15 colours; frames 1–3 are identical, frames 4–8 are the same image moved up 1 px). Claude drew half-closed and closed eyes and re-laid the frames out 8 × 1: `avatar-idle-front-blink-8x1-56.png`. This replaced the earlier plan to render the head from Blender |
    38	| Framing | Head only (with a little neck), fully frontal (my decision) |
    39	| Motion | Head: low on frames 1–3, 1 px higher on frames 4–8 (after frame 8 it drops back: the "sink"). Eyes: frame 1 open, 2 half-closed, 3 closed, 4 half-open (the same frame the head rises), 5–8 open. The blink overlaps the head's sink and rise instead of one motion finishing before the next starts (my decision: start closing the eyes on the 2nd–3rd frame after the head starts to sink) |
    40	| Frame count | 8 frames, laid out 8 × 1 |
    41	| Speed | 4 frames per second; one loop is 2 s |
    42	| Cell size | 56 × 56 px pixel art, shown at its native size in the taskbar |
    43	| Position | Far left of the taskbar, left of the window buttons |
    44	| Seam | Frame 8 goes straight back to frame 1; the first frame is not repeated |
    45	
    46	- It only displays; it decides no game state. When the tablet is put away the tablet OS canvas stops drawing, so the head is not drawn either.
    47	- Its code lives in `computer_system/tablet_os/system/pixel_head/` (part of the system UI, not an app).
    48	
    49	### The sheet: provenance and slicing
    50	
    51	| Item | Content |
    52	|---|---|
    53	| Source | Generated asset, logged under Assignment 2's rules in SOURCES.md (AVATAR-SPRITE-02). Codex (OpenAI) generated one front-facing master head with its image tool, then in code reduced it to a 56 × 56 pixel grid, copied it into 8 cells and moved it 1 px; Claude drew the two blink eye states with Pillow |
    54	| Author | Me (generated with Codex, edited by Claude at my request) |
    55	| Licence | OpenAI Terms of Use (effective 2026-01-01, read on 2026-11-22): the user owns the Output, and OpenAI assigns its rights in the Output to the user; the user must review Output before using or sharing it and must not present it as human-made. OpenAI's Sharing & Publication Policy (2022-11-14) asks that AI-generated content shared on social media be clearly marked as AI-generated. So it can go in a public repository and a published film, and README, the film and `ATTRIBUTION.md` all say the head is AI-generated (Codex image tool) and edited by Claude |
    56	| Date checked | 2026-11-22 |
    57	| Original as downloaded | Codex's `avatar-idle-front-sheet-4x2-56.png` (4 × 2, 224 × 112), committed unchanged in `design/avatar-sprite/`. The image tool's first 1254 × 1254 output was not saved; Codex kept the reduced `avatar-idle-front-master-56.png` |
    58	| Sheet used in the game | `avatar-idle-front-blink-8x1-56.png` (448 × 56), in `computer_system/tablet_os/system/pixel_head/` with the head scene and `ATTRIBUTION.md` |
    59	| Cell size | 56 × 56 px, no padding between cells |
    60	| Grid | `hframes` = 8, `vframes` = 1 |
    61	| Frame order | Left to right, 0–7, matching frames 1–8 under "Motion" |
    62	| Credits file | `ATTRIBUTION.md` next to the sheet: source, author, licence, date checked |
    63	| Registration | In the original the head sits in only two positions in its cell, low and 1 px up; that is the intended bob, not drift. The frame strip checks for any other shift |
    64	
    65	### Cycle spec
    66	
    67	| Item | Content |
    68	|---|---|
    69	| Frame count and rate | 8 frames, 4 fps |
    70	| Clip length | 2.0 s |
    71	| `Animation.step` | 0.25 s (one frame at 4 fps) |
    72	| Keys | At 0.00, 0.25, 0.50 … 1.75 s, `frame` = 0 to 7 in order |
    73	| Loop mode | `Animation.LOOP_LINEAR` |
    74	| Update mode | `Animation.UPDATE_DISCRETE` |
    75	| Seam rule (frame track) | No duplicate across the wrap: the last key is `frame` = 7 and it wraps to `frame` = 0, which differ (head height and eyes); the gap from the last key (1.75 s) to the clip's length (2.0 s) is 0.25 s, equal to the key interval |
    76	| Frame range | Only 0–7; never a cell past the 8th (the sheet has 8 cells) |
    77	
    78	## Clip: one-handed tablet raise (`tablet_raise_one_hand`, committing action)
    79	
    80	### Task
    81	
    82	From standing, the character takes the tablet off her left hip with her left hand and raises it to chest height to look at the screen. I posed the end pose in Blender (`tablet_hold_one_hand`); Claude worked out the in-between frames from the hip start pose.
    83	
    84	### Phase table
    85	
    86	Frame rate 30 fps; `Animation.step` = 1/30 s (≈ 0.0333 s, one frame). Frames 0–20, 21 frames in all, 20 / 30 ≈ 0.667 s. Each phase includes its first frame and excludes its last; the last phase includes frame 20. Frame 0 is the physics frame on which a short press changes `Humanoid`'s hold state from put away to one-handed.
    87	
    88	| Phase | Begins on | Frames | Time (s) | What the player may do | What the game reads | What the animation does |
    89	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    90	| Startup | 0 | 0–6 | 0.000–0.233 | No walking, running, jumping, aiming or interacting; can interrupt with Tab (short press = put it back, long press = switch to two hands) | Hold state = one-handed; screen dark, not clickable | 0–5: the left hand reaches for the tablet on the hip, fingers opening slightly; 5–7: the hand grips the tablet's edge and the fingers close into the grip |
    91	| Active | 7 | 7–15 | 0.233–0.533 | Same | Same | 7–10: the tablet is lifted straight up about 10 cm; 10–16: it moves forward while turning, screen towards the face; 8–16: the head slowly lowers |
    92	| Recovery | 16 | 16–20 | 0.533–0.667 | Same | Frames 16–19: screen still dark, not clickable; frame 20: screen lights and becomes clickable | 16: reaches the end pose; 18: overshoots 8 mm along the motion; 20: back on the end pose, settled |
    93	| (Afterwards: holding one-handed) | after 20 | — | — | Can walk; no running, jumping, aiming or interacting (the existing rule, unchanged) | Screen lit, clickable | Holds the end pose |
    94	
    95	**Keyed gameplay fact: on frame 20 (0.667 s, the clip's last frame) the screen lights and becomes clickable.** On frame 19 and before it is dark and not clickable; only when the clip has finished, on frame 20, does it light (my decision: "light it after it has been picked up, once the animation has finished"). The bottom-right demo tablet still slides in on its own over 0.35 s, but its screen also waits for frame 20 before it lights and becomes clickable (my decision).
    96	
    97	### What is already set up
    98	
    99	- Start pose: left hand hanging at the side, tablet on the outside of the left hip. So that the hand can reach it, the hip position of the tablet was moved 7 cm forward and 5 cm up from the first draft (about (0.29, −0.07, 0.88) m in Blender's world space). The old position was 0.417 m from the shoulder; this arm is 0.379 m long.
   100	- End pose: the tablet position, grip, elbow direction and head angle I posed; the fingers were posed by Claude (thumb on the left bezel of the screen, four fingers on the back, no back finger showing through the screen).
   101	- The tablet follows a `tablet` bone in the rig; the left hand follows the tablet through a grip bone, `tablet_grip.l`.
   102	
   103	### One authority
   104	
   105	- In the game, the tablet (`TabletDevice`) hangs under a `BoneAttachment3D` that follows the `tablet` bone; only the animation decides where the tablet is.
   106	- The code in `humanoid.gd` that slides the tablet between three slots over 0.35 s (`_update_tablet_visual()`), and the three slots `TabletHipSlot` / `TabletOneHandSlot` / `TabletTwoHandSlot`, are removed.
   107	- The screen no longer lights when "the tablet has slid into place"; it lights when the clip reaches frame 20 (its last frame).
   108	
   109	### Testable rules
   110	
   111	- While raising (frames 0–20): no walking, running or jumping.
   112	- Interrupts: if the player presses a key mid-raise to change state, the current clip is **cancelled and the character blends from its current pose into the next state's animation**. Example: a long press halfway through the one-handed raise (switch to two hands) immediately blends into the two-handed state from the current pose, without finishing the one-handed raise first.
   113	  - The blend from the current pose takes 6 frames (0.2 s).
   114	  - An interrupted one-handed raise never reaches frame 20, so the screen does not light (I confirmed this); if the interrupt goes to two hands, the two-handed rule decides when it lights.
   115	
   116	### Import settings (where the loop mode lives)
   117	
   118	- One `.glb` (character + skeleton + actions) exported from `xz_anim.blend` into `assets/characters/main_character/`, with an `ATTRIBUTION.md` beside it (commissioned for this project, used with permission). The reference tablet model in Blender is not exported; only the `tablet` bone's animation is.
   119	- Each action's loop mode is set in the importer's per-animation settings (saved in the `.glb.import` file), not edited by hand in the imported scene: `tablet_raise_one_hand` = no loop (`Animation.LOOP_NONE`); the hold poses do not loop either.
   120	- Proof that it survives: delete the `.godot/` import cache, run `--import` again, and run the read-back test that reads the loop mode.
   121	- To handle on export: the character is scaled up 5.07× in Blender (otherwise the tablet hanging on the bone would be scaled up too); Blender and Godot use different axis conventions (the tablet may need a fixed rotation).
   122	
   123	## State machine (the tablet-raise side)
   124	
   125	(I agreed to this, 2026-11-22.) The tablet logic I already built in `humanoid.gd` (put away / one-handed / two-handed, what a short and a long press do) does not change. This state machine is a separate layer: an animation state machine that only decides which animation plays, following that logic. It is the character's `AnimationTree` with an `AnimationNodeStateMachine` as its root. It is the one authority over the skeleton; because the tablet follows the `tablet` bone, it is also the one authority over the tablet's position.
   126	
   127	| State | Plays |
   128	|---|---|
   129	| `hip` (put away) | The put-away hold pose (tablet on the left hip; frame 0 of the raise) |
   130	| `raise_1h` (raising one-handed) | `tablet_raise_one_hand`, frames 0–20, no loop |
   131	| `hold_1h` (holding one-handed) | The one-handed hold pose (my end pose) |
   132	| `hold_2h` (holding two-handed) | The two-handed hold pose. I have not posed it yet, so the one-handed hold pose stands in for it (my decision: finish the assignment minimum first, then add animation); it will be replaced in a dated revision |
   133	
   134	The transitions follow the hold-state table in `humanoid.gd` (`_next_tablet_hold()`: put away + short press → one-handed, + long press → two-handed; one-handed + short → put away, + long → two-handed; two-handed + short → one-handed, + long → put away):
   135	
   136	| From → to | Condition | Cross-fade | Switch |
   137	|---|---|---|---|
   138	| `hip` → `raise_1h` | Hold state becomes one-handed | 0 (same start pose) | Immediate |
   139	| `raise_1h` → `hold_1h` | Clip finished (frame 20) | 0 | At end (`SWITCH_MODE_AT_END`) |
   140	| `raise_1h` → `hip` | Hold state becomes put away (short press mid-raise) | 6 frames (0.2 s) | Immediate (interrupt) |
   141	| `raise_1h` → `hold_2h` | Hold state becomes two-handed (long press mid-raise) | 0.2 s | Immediate (interrupt) |
   142	| `hip` → `hold_2h` | Hold state becomes two-handed | 0.2 s | Immediate |
   143	| `hold_1h` → `hold_2h` | Hold state becomes two-handed | 0.2 s | Immediate |
   144	| `hold_2h` → `hold_1h` | Hold state becomes one-handed | 0.2 s | Immediate |
   145	| `hold_1h` → `hip` | Hold state becomes put away | 0.2 s | Immediate |
   146	| `hold_2h` → `hip` | Hold state becomes put away | 0.2 s | Immediate |
   147	
   148	- Apart from the at-end transition, every transition uses `ADVANCE_MODE_AUTO` with an advance expression such as `get_tablet_hold() == 1`. The expression is evaluated against `advance_expression_base_node`, which is set to the character's root node `Humanoid` (`humanoid.gd`); without it the expression silently fails.
   149	- The `AnimationTree` only reads the hold state; it writes no game state (presentation reads, never writes).
   150	- Screen lighting: every physics frame `Humanoid` reads which state the state machine is in. The rule is always "light once in place" (my decision): it lights when the raise finishes and the machine enters `hold_1h`; for every other transition the screen is dark during the 6-frame blend and lights when the blend ends and the machine is in `hold_1h` / `hold_2h` (so switching between one and two hands now goes dark for 0.2 s, unlike the current game); on the frame the state becomes `hip` the screen goes dark (as now).
   151	
   152	## The two clocks
   153	
   154	| Node | `callback_mode_process` | Advances on |
   155	|---|---|---|
   156	| Character `AnimationTree` | `AnimationMixer.ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_PROCESS_IDLE` (default; my decision) | Process tick |
   157	| Head `AnimationPlayer` | `AnimationMixer.ANIMATION_CALLBACK_MODE_PROCESS_IDLE` (default) | Process tick |
   158	
   159	- The project uses no `AnimatedSprite2D` (it can only advance on the process tick and has no such setting).
   160	- The game reads one keyed gameplay fact: "the raise has finished → the screen lights and is clickable". `Humanoid` reads it on the physics tick (`apply_intent()` is called by the brain from `_physics_process()`).
   161	- The character's `AnimationTree` advances on the process tick and the game reads on the physics tick, so the clocks differ. If the state machine enters `hold_1h` during a process frame, the game sees it on the next physics frame. Largest disagreement: the larger of one rendered frame and one physics frame (1/60 s ≈ 0.017 s). At 60 fps rendering about 0.017 s; if rendering drops to 30 fps, about 0.033 s (one rendered frame then advances the clip by 2 frames).
   162	- Headless tests run with `--fixed-fps`, where a process frame and a physics frame are the same length, so the tests are deterministic; the real-game disagreement can only be judged in play.
   163	- The head clip produces no gameplay fact, so its tick does not affect the game.
   164	- No method track is used to make the clocks agree (method tracks are deferred).
   165	
   166	## Boundaries
   167	
   168	Unchanged: collision, movement speeds, input bindings, jumping, interaction, the hold-state table in `humanoid.gd`, my Assignment 5 shaders (the two hand-written files in `shaders/`), my Assignment 6 effects (both dusts), every other object in the base scene, and the rest of the tablet OS.
   169	
   170	Changed by this brief (only these):
   171	
   172	1. The tablet's position is driven by the animation: the 0.35 s slide in `_update_tablet_visual()` and the three slots (`TabletHipSlot` / `TabletOneHandSlot` / `TabletTwoHandSlot`) are removed, and `TabletDevice` hangs under a `BoneAttachment3D` on the `tablet` bone.
   173	2. The screen-lighting rule: from "the tablet has slid into place" to "the one-handed raise has finished (frame 20)", plus the "light once in place" rule for the other transitions.
   174	3. No walking, running or jumping while raising (frames 0–20). This is new; the one-handed rule after the raise is unchanged.
   175	4. The character's capsule look is replaced by the xz model (under `Visual/human_model`; the collision capsule is unchanged).
   176	5. Existing test expectations that depend on the 0.35 s slide change: the take-out, put-away and mid-way interrupt cases in `tests/screen_glow_check.gd`, and the "screen stays lit between one and two hands" case (Claude lists them one by one before writing the pins).
   177	6. The bottom-right demo tablet (`screen_tablet.gd`, which slides in by code): its 0.35 s slide is unchanged; its screen now waits for frame 20 of the raise before it lights and becomes clickable (my decision).
   178	7. The pixel head is added at the far left of the tablet OS taskbar.
   179	
   180	Presentation (animation, the pixel head, the demo tablet) may read game state; it never writes it.
   181	
   182	## The evidence split
   183	
   184	| Rule | Checked by |
   185	|---|---|
   186	| The head track points at `Sprite2D:frame`, discrete updates, frames only 0–7, key times, `LOOP_LINEAR`, `step` = 0.25, no duplicate across the seam | Read-back test |

     6	# Examples: ./scripts/run-test.sh a3_asset_check.gd 60
     7	#           ./scripts/run-test.sh cost_effects.gd 60 300
     8	# It does six things:
     9	#   1. Wraps Godot in timeout: if a test script errors before quit(), headless Godot keeps running; it is killed when the time is up (exit code 124 = hung)
    10	#   2. When the second argument is a frame rate, pins it with --fixed-fps: every frame's delta is 1/fps, whatever the machine's speed
    11	#      When the second argument is realtime, the frame rate is not pinned: for tests that wait on audio (timers follow game time, audio follows the real clock)
    12	#   3. An optional third argument sets the timeout in seconds (120 when left out), for the long-running cost script
    13	#   4. Keeps a copy of the output as a log in logs/
    14	#   5. Fails when the log contains SHADER ERROR or SCRIPT ERROR (Godot can exit 0 even after such errors)
    15	#   6. New in A7: also fails when the log contains Failed loading resource (a clip whose scene or sheet will not load prints it, and the test would otherwise carry on against a half-built scene)
    16	
    17	# ============================================================
    18	# Setting: a pipeline fails if any command in it fails (otherwise only the final tee counts, and tee always succeeds)
    19	# ============================================================
    20	set -o pipefail
    21	
    22	# ============================================================
    23	# The two changes from the template
    24	# ============================================================
    25	# 1. Godot project folder: godot/ in this repository, project-survival-shooting/ in my local working folder. Use whichever exists
    26	if [ -f godot/project.godot ]; then
    27		project="godot"
    28	else
    29		project="project-survival-shooting"
    30	fi
    31	# 2. Godot program: can be set with the GODOT environment variable; if unset, use the console build godot_console when it exists (Windows), otherwise godot
    32	#    (on Windows the GUI build godot.exe does not send its output into a pipe, so the console build comes first)
    33	if [ -z "$GODOT" ]; then
    34		if command -v godot_console > /dev/null; then
    35			GODOT="godot_console"
    36		else
    37			GODOT="godot"
    38		fi

    43	# ============================================================
    44	if [ "$2" = "realtime" ]; then

    46		tag="realtime"  # The log name says realtime

    49		tag="${2}fps"  # The log name says the frame rate, e.g. 60fps

    54	# ============================================================
    55	mkdir -p logs

   162			_tablet_screen_lit = false
   163		elif _tablet_move_progress == TABLET_MOVE_DONE:
   164			_tablet_screen_lit = true
   165		_tablet.set_screen_lit(_tablet_screen_lit)
   166	
   167	
   168	
   169	## Lookup: tablet state -> which slot the tablet belongs in. Calculation only, changes nothing. Called by _update_tablet_visual().
   170	func _get_tablet_slot(hold: TabletHold) -> Marker3D:
   171		match hold:
   172			TabletHold.ONE_HAND:
   173				return _tablet_one_hand_slot
   174			TabletHold.TWO_HAND:
   175				return _tablet_two_hand_slot
   176			_:  # The remaining case: NONE (not holding the tablet)
   177				return _tablet_hip_slot
   178	
   179	
   180	## apply_intent() calls this when the intent's interact is true: find something nearby to interact with and ask it to do its thing.
   181	## Whether interaction is allowed is answered by that thing's own can_interact() (a query point, rule 3); what happens is decided by its own interact().
   182	## If several are nearby at once, we interact only with the nearest one, so one press of F does exactly one thing.
   183	func _try_interact() -> void:
   184		var nearest: Node3D = null  # First, we have not found anything to interact with yet
   185		var nearest_distance := INF  # The nearest distance starts at infinity, so the first one we find is always nearer
   186		for target in get_tree().get_nodes_in_group(INTERACTABLE_GROUP):  # We look at everything in the interactable group,
   187			if not target.can_interact(self):  # and if it says "you are too far away to interact with me",
   188				continue  # we skip it and look at the next one
   189			var distance := global_position.distance_to(target.global_position)  # Otherwise, we work out how far it is from the body
   190			if distance < nearest_distance:  # If it is nearer than everything found so far,
   191				nearest = target  # we remember it as "the nearest one"
   192				nearest_distance = distance  # and remember its distance, for the next ones to compare against
   193		if nearest != null:  # Finally, if we found one,
   194			nearest.interact(self)  # we ask it to do its thing; the switch receives this request and then switches the lights
   195	
   196	
   197	## Shows or hides this body's character model (only human_model is hidden, not the tablet, so the tablet in hand stays visible in first person).
   198	## Only affects the picture on the machine that calls it; not game state (rule 5).
   199	## Called by the player brain when switching to first person; in co-op, teammates' machines don't call it, so they still see you.
   200	func set_visual_visible(visible_locally: bool) -> void:
   201		_human_model.visible = visible_locally
   202	
   203	
   204	## Returns the current tablet state. The brain uses it to decide which inputs may go into the intent this frame.
   205	func get_tablet_hold() -> TabletHold:
   206		return _tablet_hold
   207	
   208	
   209	## The player brain calls this at the start of the game to get the tablet in this character's hand, so it can hand the tablet system's picture to its screen.
   210	## The brain uses it only to hand over the picture (presentation); where the tablet is held and whether it is lit are still decided only by the body itself.
   211	func get_tablet() -> TabletDevice:
   212		return _tablet  # We hand out the tablet in this character's hand
   213	
   214	
   215	## Switches the tablet state by this frame's tablet key result, and emits tablet_hold_changed when the state changed.
   216	## Called by apply_intent() every physics frame; does nothing when press is NONE.
   217	func _apply_tablet_press(press: CharacterIntent.TabletPress) -> void:
   218		if press == CharacterIntent.TabletPress.NONE:
   219			return
   220		var old_hold := _tablet_hold
   221		_tablet_hold = _next_tablet_hold(old_hold, press)
   222		tablet_hold_changed.emit(old_hold, _tablet_hold)
   223	
   224	
   225	## Looks up the switching table (design document section 5.8): current state + short or long press -> new state. Calculation only, changes nothing.
   226	func _next_tablet_hold(current: TabletHold, press: CharacterIntent.TabletPress) -> TabletHold:
   227		var is_long := press == CharacterIntent.TabletPress.LONG
   228		match current:  # match is the switch of other languages
   229			TabletHold.NONE:
   230				return TabletHold.TWO_HAND if is_long else TabletHold.ONE_HAND
   231			TabletHold.ONE_HAND:
   232				return TabletHold.TWO_HAND if is_long else TabletHold.NONE
   233			_:  # The remaining case: TWO_HAND (_ is switch's default)
   234				return TabletHold.NONE if is_long else TabletHold.ONE_HAND

1	# ============================================================
     2	# Class declaration: class name, what it extends, what the whole script does
     3	# ============================================================
     4	class_name PlayerController  # Global class name: the player brain
     5	extends Node3D  # Extends Node3D: so the camera under it moves along with the body
     6	## Player brain (code rule 7a): reads keyboard and mouse, turns the local camera, packs the input into an intent, and hands it to the body.
     7	## Attached under the humanoid body (Humanoid); its parent is the body it drives.
     8	## The mouse turns only the camera, not the character; the body decides its facing from the move direction.
     9	
    10	# ============================================================
    11	# Constants: values defined once that never change
    12	# ============================================================
    13	const PLAYER_GROUP := &"players"  # Every player body joins this group (rule 6: never assume there is only one player)
    14	const THIRD_PERSON_BLEND := 0.0  # View blend value: camera fully at the third-person position
    15	const FIRST_PERSON_BLEND := 1.0  # View blend value: camera fully at the first-person position
    16	
    17	# ============================================================
    18	# Exported variables (@export): feel parameters shown in the Inspector and tuned there
    19	# ============================================================
    20	## Camera feel parameters (code rule 1a): tuned in the Inspector, not hard-coded.
    21	@export var mouse_sensitivity: float = 0.0025  # Radians the view turns per pixel of mouse movement
    22	@export_range(-89.0, 0.0) var pitch_min_degrees: float = -70.0  # How far down you can look, in degrees
    23	@export_range(0.0, 89.0) var pitch_max_degrees: float = 60.0  # How far up you can look, in degrees
    24	@export var tablet_long_press_seconds: float = 0.4  # Seconds the tablet key must be held to count as a long press; released sooner = short press
    25	@export var aim_transition_seconds: float = 0.15  # Seconds for the camera to move from third person to the eyes when aiming with the right button (0 = cut instantly)
    26	@export var tablet_transition_seconds: float = 0.35  # Seconds for the camera to move from third person to the eyes when holding the tablet in both hands
    27	@export_range(0.0, 1.0) var hide_body_at_blend: float = 0.7  # Hide your own body once the view blend passes this value (the camera is nearly inside the head)
    28	@export_range(-89.0, 89.0) var tablet_view_pitch_degrees: float = -20.0  # First-person camera pitch while holding the tablet in both hands: -20 = looking down at the tablet a little (0 = level, negative = down)
    29	
    30	# ============================================================
    31	# Member variables: state used inside this script (leading underscore = internal to this script)
    32	# ============================================================
    33	var _look_delta := Vector2.ZERO  # Mouse movement accumulated between two physics frames, processed together in the physics frame
    34	var _tablet_held_seconds := 0.0  # Seconds the tablet key has been held; reset on release
    35	var _view_blend := THIRD_PERSON_BLEND  # View blend value (the "slider"): 0 = third person, 1 = first person, in between = mid-transition
    36	var _view_target := THIRD_PERSON_BLEND  # Where the slider is heading: 0 or 1. The slider is pushed toward it a little every frame
    37	var _view_transition_seconds := 0.0  # How long this transition takes. Set when entering first person, reused when going back (leave the way you came in)
    38	var _view_is_tablet := false  # Whether this first-person view is because of the two-handed tablet: yes = the camera ends up level, facing the tablet. Reused when going back
    39	
    40	# ============================================================
    41	# Node references (@onready): nodes used in the scene
    42	# ============================================================
    43	# @onready: assigned after the node enters the scene tree and its children are ready
    44	@onready var _body: Humanoid = get_parent() as Humanoid  # Parent node: the humanoid body this brain drives
    45	@onready var _camera_pivot: Node3D = $CameraPivot  # Camera pivot: looking left/right turns its Y axis, up/down turns its X axis
    46	@onready var _spring_arm: SpringArm3D = $CameraPivot/SpringArm3D  # The camera arm that shortens against walls
    47	@onready var _third_person_position: Marker3D = $CameraPivot/SpringArm3D/ThirdPersonCameraPosition  # Where the camera belongs in third person: at the arm's end, dodging walls with it
    48	@onready var _first_person_position: Marker3D = $CameraPivot/FirstPersonCameraPosition  # Where the camera belongs in first person: the eyes
    49	@onready var _camera: Camera3D = $PlayerCamera  # The only camera that actually renders; placed between the two positions above every frame
    50	@onready var _screen_tablet: ScreenTablet = $ScreenTabletLayer/SubViewportContainer/SubViewport/ScreenTablet  # The demo tablet in the lower right: it slides in from the right edge of the screen when the tablet is held one-handed, and it is the one the player operates with the mouse later; we tell it in _on_tablet_hold_changed() whether to come out or go back
    51	@onready var _tablet_os_viewport: SubViewport = $TabletOSViewport  # The tablet OS canvas: the whole game has only this one tablet OS drawn on it; _ready() hands the picture it draws to the screens of both tablets
    52	@onready var _screen_tablet_container: SubViewportContainer = $ScreenTabletLayer/SubViewportContainer  # The frame that lays the demo tablet's small 3D world over the game picture; the mouse position must first be converted to a position inside it
    53	@onready var _screen_tablet_camera: Camera3D = $ScreenTabletLayer/SubViewportContainer/SubViewport/ScreenTabletCamera  # The camera that films the demo tablet; we shoot a line from it through the mouse position and see where it hits the screen
    54	
    55	
    56	# ============================================================
    57	# Engine callbacks: functions Godot calls automatically at set times (the entry points; GDScript has no main)
    58	# ============================================================
    59	## Called by Godot: runs once after the node and its children have entered the scene tree; used for setup.
    60	func _ready() -> void:
    61		_body.add_to_group(PLAYER_GROUP)  # Put the body in the players group; monsters will pick targets from this group
    62		_spring_arm.add_excluded_object(_body.get_rid())  # When the camera arm checks for walls, ignore the body's own capsule
    63		_camera.make_current()  # Render with the player camera (replaces preview_camera in the scene)
    64		Input.mouse_mode = Input.MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED  # Lock and hide the mouse; mouse movement only turns the view
    65		_body.tablet_hold_changed.connect(_on_tablet_hold_changed)  # When the tablet state changes, switch the mouse (locked / visible)
    66		if not _body.is_node_ready():  # The brain is a child of the body, and Godot readies the children before the parent, so at this moment the body may not be ready yet and may not know which tablet is in its hand
    67			await _body.ready  # If so, we wait for the body to emit ready (it is ready now) before going on
    68		var tablet_os_image := _tablet_os_viewport.get_texture()  # We get the picture of the tablet OS canvas; every time the canvas draws a frame, this picture changes with it
    69		_body.get_tablet().set_screen_image(tablet_os_image)  # Then we hand the picture to the screen of the tablet in the body's hand
    70		_screen_tablet.set_screen_image(tablet_os_image)  # Then we hand the same picture to the demo tablet in the lower right; both show the same single tablet OS (GDD 5.8)
    71	
    72	
    73	## Called by Godot: runs for every input event (keyboard, mouse) that the UI or other nodes did not handle.
    74	## Only handles the mouse here: while the tablet is held, it hands the mouse to the tablet OS; otherwise it records mouse movement, Esc frees the mouse, and clicking the view locks it again.
    75	func _unhandled_input(event: InputEvent) -> void:
    76		if event is InputEventMouse and _is_holding_tablet():  # If this is a mouse action (movement or a button) and the tablet is held now (one-handed or two-handed)
    77			_send_mouse_to_tablet_os(event)  # we hand it to the tablet OS
    78			return  # While the tablet is held the mouse is only for clicking the tablet, so we skip turning the view and locking the mouse below
    79		if event is InputEventMouseMotion and Input.mouse_mode == Input.MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED:
    80			_look_delta += (event as InputEventMouseMotion).relative  # Accumulate mouse movement, processed in the physics frame
    81		elif event.is_action_pressed(&"ui_cancel"):  # ui_cancel is a built-in Godot action, Esc by default
    82			Input.mouse_mode = Input.MOUSE_MODE_VISIBLE  # Free the mouse
    83		elif event is InputEventMouseButton and event.pressed and Input.mouse_mode != Input.MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED:
    84			if not _is_holding_tablet():  # While holding the tablet the mouse is for clicking the tablet, so a click must not lock it again
    85				Input.mouse_mode = Input.MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED  # Click the view while the mouse is free to lock it again
    86	
    87	
    88	## Called by Godot: runs once per physics frame (60 times a second by default); delta is the seconds since the last frame.
    89	## First turns the local camera, then reads the intent and hands it to the body, and finally decides which view the camera heads for from the aim and tablet state.
    90	func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
    91		_rotate_camera()
    92		var intent := _read_intent(delta)
    93		_body.apply_intent(intent, delta)
    94		_update_view(intent.aim)
    95	
    96	
    97	## Called by Godot: runs once per rendered frame (follows the frame rate, so more or fewer times than physics frames), after this frame's physics frame.
    98	## First pushes the slider toward its target a little, then places the camera. It is here rather than in the physics frame so the camera arm has finished dodging walls this frame.
    99	func _process(delta: float) -> void:
   100		_move_view_blend(delta)
   101		_update_camera()
   102	
   103	
   104	# ============================================================
   105	# Feature functions: our own functions, called by the callbacks above
   106	# ============================================================
   107	## Turns the local camera by the mouse movement accumulated over this time: left/right turns the pivot's Y axis, up/down its X axis.
   108	## Turns only the camera, not the character. The camera is local "presentation", so it is not part of the intent (rule 5).
   109	func _rotate_camera() -> void:
   110		_camera_pivot.rotation.y -= _look_delta.x * mouse_sensitivity  # Mouse right, view right (negative direction around Y)
   111		_camera_pivot.rotation.x = clampf(  # clampf: limits a value between a minimum and a maximum
   112			_camera_pivot.rotation.x - _look_delta.y * mouse_sensitivity,  # Mouse up, look up
   113			deg_to_rad(pitch_min_degrees), deg_to_rad(pitch_max_degrees))  # Degrees converted to radians
   114		_look_delta = Vector2.ZERO  # The mouse movement is used up; reset and start accumulating again
   115	
   116	
   117	## Reads this frame's keys and camera facing into a CharacterIntent. Reads input only, moves nothing.
   118	## Filtered by the tablet state (design document section 5.8): whatever is not put in the intent, the body does not do this frame.
   119	##   Not holding the tablet: everything is allowed.
   120	##   One-handed: walking only; no sprint, jump, aim or interact (shooting and using medicine will go here later too).
   121	##   Two-handed: operating the tablet only; walk, sprint, jump and aim are not put in the intent.
   122	func _read_intent(delta: float) -> CharacterIntent:
   123		var intent := CharacterIntent.new()  # Everything in a new intent defaults to "don't" (zero, false)
   124		var hold := _body.get_tablet_hold()  # Ask the body: is the tablet held now, and how?
   125		intent.look_yaw = _camera_pivot.global_rotation.y  # The player's "look direction" = the camera's left/right facing in the world
   126		if hold != Humanoid.TabletHold.TWO_HAND:  # Walking only when not holding the tablet in both hands
   127			# get_vector combines four direction keys into a 2D vector whose length stays at most 1 when moving diagonally
   128			intent.move = Input.get_vector(&"move_left", &"move_right", &"move_back", &"move_forward")
   129		if hold == Humanoid.TabletHold.NONE:  # Sprint, jump and aim only with no tablet in hand
   130			intent.sprint = Input.is_action_pressed(&"sprint")  # True for as long as it is held
   131			intent.jump = Input.is_action_just_pressed(&"jump")  # True only on the frame it was just pressed
   132			intent.aim = Input.is_action_pressed(&"aim")  # True for as long as the right button is held
   133			intent.interact = Input.is_action_just_pressed(&"interact")  # If the player has just pressed F this frame, we write "wants to interact" into the intent; holding the key does not count again
   134		intent.tablet_press = _read_tablet_press(delta)  # The tablet key is read in every state, or the tablet could never be put away
   135		return intent
   136	
   137	
   138	## Decides whether the tablet key (Tab) was a short press, a long press, or neither this frame. Called once per physics frame by _read_intent().
   139	## While held, time accumulates; the frame that crosses the long-press time counts as one long press. Released before the long-press time, the release frame counts as a short press.
   140	func _read_tablet_press(delta: float) -> CharacterIntent.TabletPress:
   141		if Input.is_action_pressed(&"tablet"):  # Still held
   142			var before := _tablet_held_seconds
   143			_tablet_held_seconds += delta
   144			if before < tablet_long_press_seconds and _tablet_held_seconds >= tablet_long_press_seconds:
   145				return CharacterIntent.TabletPress.LONG  # Only the crossing frame matches, so holding on does not count again
   146			return CharacterIntent.TabletPress.NONE
   147		# Not held: it was held (time above 0) but not for the long-press time, so it was just released as a short press
   148		var is_short := _tablet_held_seconds > 0.0 and _tablet_held_seconds < tablet_long_press_seconds
   149		_tablet_held_seconds = 0.0  # Reset, ready for the next press
   150		return CharacterIntent.TabletPress.SHORT if is_short else CharacterIntent.TabletPress.NONE
   151	
   152	
   153	## While the tablet is held, _unhandled_input() calls this every time it receives a mouse action (movement or a button):
   154	## we work out which point on the tablet screen the mouse points at, turn this mouse action into a position on the tablet OS canvas, and hand it to the tablet OS.
   155	## When the mouse is not pointing at the screen we hand over nothing. This is only the local input method; what happens inside the tablet OS (opening windows and so on) is decided by the tablet OS itself.
   156	func _send_mouse_to_tablet_os(event: InputEventMouse) -> void:
   157		var screen_uv := _get_mouse_screen_uv(event)  # First we ask: where on the tablet screen does the mouse point (0 to 1); one-handed and two-handed each have their own way of working it out
   158		if screen_uv == TabletDevice.NOT_ON_SCREEN:  # If it did not hit the screen (the click is on the frame or outside the tablet)
   159			return  # we hand over nothing, and this click does not count (GDD 5.8: only a click on this tablet's screen counts)
   160		var os_event := event.duplicate() as InputEventMouse  # If it hit, we make a copy of this mouse action and leave the original alone
   161		os_event.position = screen_uv * Vector2(_tablet_os_viewport.size)  # We change the copy's position to a pixel on the tablet OS canvas: screen position × canvas size (1280 × 768)
   162		os_event.global_position = os_event.position  # There is no outer layer around the canvas, so the "global position" is the same as the position
   163		_tablet_os_viewport.push_input(os_event, true)  # Finally we hand it to the tablet OS canvas; the desktop icons, buttons and windows on the canvas react as if a real mouse had clicked them
   164	
   165	
   166	## _send_mouse_to_tablet_os() calls this: it works out where the mouse points on the screen of "the tablet that can be operated right now".
   167	## When holding the tablet one-handed, the one that can be operated is the demo tablet in the lower right (using the small camera that films it); when holding it two-handed, it is the one in hand (using the player's main camera). If the mouse is not on the screen, it returns TabletDevice.NOT_ON_SCREEN.
   168	func _get_mouse_screen_uv(event: InputEventMouse) -> Vector2:
   169		if _body.get_tablet_hold() == Humanoid.TabletHold.ONE_HAND:  # If the tablet is held one-handed now
   170			var event_in_box := _screen_tablet_container.make_input_local(event) as InputEventMouse  # we first convert the mouse position to "the position inside the demo tablet's frame"
   171			var mouse_in_view := event_in_box.position / _screen_tablet_container.stretch_shrink  # then to a pixel in the small 3D world's picture (the frame shrank the picture by some factor, so we divide it back here)
   172			var small_ray_origin := _screen_tablet_camera.project_ray_origin(mouse_in_view)  # Then, on the camera that films the demo tablet, we find the start of the line that passes through this pixel
   173			var small_ray_direction := _screen_tablet_camera.project_ray_normal(mouse_in_view)  # and the direction of this line
   174			return _screen_tablet.get_screen_uv(small_ray_origin, small_ray_direction)  # Finally we ask the demo tablet: where on your screen does this line hit
   175		var ray_origin := _camera.project_ray_origin(event.position)  # Otherwise (holding the tablet two-handed), we shoot a line from the player's main camera through the mouse position; this is its start
   176		var ray_direction := _camera.project_ray_normal(event.position)  # and the direction of this line
   177		return _body.get_tablet().get_screen_uv(ray_origin, ray_direction)  # We ask the tablet in hand: where on your screen does this line hit
   178	
   179	
   180	## Whether the local player is holding the tablet now (one-handed or two-handed both count).
   181	## Called by _unhandled_input() and _on_tablet_hold_changed().
   182	func _is_holding_tablet() -> bool:
   183		return _body.get_tablet_hold() != Humanoid.TabletHold.NONE
   184	
   185	
   186	## Switches the mouse after the tablet state changes: holding the tablet = show the mouse (for clicking the tablet), tablet put away = lock the mouse (for turning the view).
   187	## Called by the body's tablet_hold_changed signal (connected in _ready()). The mouse is only the local input method, not game state.
   188	## Once the mouse is visible, _unhandled_input() stops accumulating mouse movement, so the view naturally stops turning.
   189	## We also tell the demo tablet in the lower right whether to come out or go back: it comes out only while the tablet is held one-handed.
   190	## Finally we switch the tablet OS canvas on or off: while the tablet is held it draws every frame, while the tablet is put away it does not draw (GDD 5.8: put away = powered off, costs no performance).
   191	func _on_tablet_hold_changed(_old_hold: Humanoid.TabletHold, new_hold: Humanoid.TabletHold) -> void:
   192		_look_delta = Vector2.ZERO  # Drop mouse movement not yet used before the switch, so the view doesn't jerk when taking the tablet
   193		if _is_holding_tablet():
   194			Input.mouse_mode = Input.MOUSE_MODE_VISIBLE  # Show the mouse; it can move freely on screen
   195		else:
   196			Input.mouse_mode = Input.MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED  # Lock and hide the mouse; back to turning the view
   197		_screen_tablet.set_shown(new_hold == Humanoid.TabletHold.ONE_HAND)  # If the new state is one-handed, we let the demo tablet come out; otherwise (put away or two-handed) it goes back off screen
   198		if _is_holding_tablet():  # If the tablet is held now (one-handed or two-handed)
   199			_tablet_os_viewport.render_target_update_mode = SubViewport.UPDATE_ALWAYS  # we let the tablet OS canvas draw every frame, so the screens of both tablets show a live picture
   200		else:  # Otherwise (the tablet has been put away)
   201			_tablet_os_viewport.render_target_update_mode = SubViewport.UPDATE_DISABLED  # we stop the canvas drawing, saving the graphics card's work; the screen is dark anyway, so there is no visible difference
   202	
   203	
   204	## Decides whether the camera should head for first or third person (only sets the target, does not move the camera).
   205	## Two-handed tablet or right button held = first person, otherwise third person. This only affects the local picture, not game state (rule 5).
   206	func _update_view(aiming: bool) -> void:
   207		if _body.get_tablet_hold() == Humanoid.TabletHold.TWO_HAND:
   208			_view_target = FIRST_PERSON_BLEND
   209			_view_transition_seconds = tablet_transition_seconds  # Raising the tablet: a little slower
   210			_view_is_tablet = true  # Raising the tablet: the camera ends up level
   211		elif aiming:
   212			_view_target = FIRST_PERSON_BLEND
   213			_view_transition_seconds = aim_transition_seconds  # Aiming: must be fast, or shooting feels "sticky"
   214			_view_is_tablet = false  # Aiming: the camera keeps the player's own look direction
   215		else:
   216			_view_target = THIRD_PERSON_BLEND  # Back to third person: transition time and _view_is_tablet unchanged, leave the way you came in
   217	
   218

    29	@onready var _this_pc_icon: DesktopIcon = $Desktop/ThisPCIcon  # The "This PC" icon on the desktop; when the player double-clicks it, a new This PC window opens
    30	@onready var _window_layer: Control = $WindowLayer  # Window layer: every open window is placed here; it sits between the desktop and the taskbar, so windows cover the desktop but not the taskbar
    31	@onready var _taskbar: ColorRect = $Taskbar  # The taskbar at the bottom of the screen; the bottom edge of the window layer must line up with its top edge
    32	@onready var _taskbar_buttons: HBoxContainer = $Taskbar/Row/TaskbarButtons  # The row of window buttons in the taskbar; each time a window opens, we put a button here, and it lines them up left to right on its own, filling the space to the left of "Show desktop"
    33	@onready var _show_desktop_button: Button = $Taskbar/Row/ShowDesktopButton  # The "Show desktop" button at the far right of the taskbar; when the player clicks it, we minimise every window
    34	@onready var _window_limit_dialog: AcceptDialog = $WindowLimitDialog  # The "too many windows" dialog; normally hidden, we pop it up when 15 are open and the player tries to open another
    35	
    36	# ============================================================
    37	# Engine callbacks: functions Godot calls automatically at certain moments (they act as the entry points; GDScript has no main)
    38	# ============================================================
    39	## Godot calls this once after the tablet OS and its children are all ready: we line up the bottom of the window layer with the taskbar, make the "in use" button background, then start listening for the "This PC" icon being double-clicked and the "Show desktop" button being clicked.
    40	func _ready() -> void:
    41		_window_layer.offset_bottom = _taskbar.offset_top  # First we pull the bottom edge of the window layer up to the top edge of the taskbar; the taskbar height is filled in only once, on the taskbar, and this follows it
    42		_active_button_style = StyleBoxFlat.new()  # Then we make a new button background, just for the button "in use"
    43		_active_button_style.bg_color = active_button_color  # We paint it the colour filled in the Inspector; later _update_active_button() lends it to the button of the top window
    44		_this_pc_icon.activated.connect(_on_this_pc_icon_activated)  # Then we tell the icon: as soon as it is double-clicked, call our _on_this_pc_icon_activated()
    45		_show_desktop_button.pressed.connect(_on_show_desktop_button_pressed)  # Finally we tell the "Show desktop" button: as soon as it is clicked, call our _on_show_desktop_button_pressed()
    46	
    47	# ============================================================
    48	# Functions: called by others, or called inside this script
    49	# ============================================================
    50	## Called when the player double-clicks the "This PC" icon on the desktop (the icon emits activated): we build a new This PC window, put it in the window layer, make it fill the layer, then open it.
    51	## This PC is the file manager and may have several instances (GDD 5.2), so each double-click builds a new one.
    52	func _on_this_pc_icon_activated() -> void:
    53		if not _can_open_window():  # First we ask whether another window may still be opened; if it is already full
    54			_window_limit_dialog.popup_centered()  # we pop up "Too many windows, please close some first" in the middle of the screen; when the player clicks "OK" it closes itself
    55			return  # and then we build nothing and stop here
    56		var window: ThisPCWindow = this_pc_window_scene.instantiate()  # If we can still open one, we build a new window from the window scene file; it is not in the scene tree yet, so the player cannot see it
    57		_window_layer.add_child(window)  # Then we put it in the window layer; at that moment Godot calls its _ready(), and only then can it find its own DriveList and × button
    58		window.set_anchors_and_offsets_preset(Control.PRESET_FULL_RECT)  # Then we make it fill the whole window layer (the whole area above the taskbar); every window is fixed at this size (GDD 5.2)
    59		window.minimize_requested.connect(_on_window_minimize_requested.bind(window))  # We put our _on_window_minimize_requested on this window's "I want to minimise" list, along with the window itself, so when we are called we know which one to hide
    60		# Temporary: there is no "player gets their own tablet" yet, so for now we use the test tablet in the backend fake data; later the player will hand their own tablet's ID to the tablet OS
    61		window.open(FileService.get_test_tablet_uid(), FileService)  # Then we tell the new window which tablet to show and that its data entry point is the backend FileService; the window lists the drives at once
    62		var button := _add_taskbar_button(_this_pc_icon.name_key, window)  # Then we put a button for this window on the taskbar, with the same name as written under the desktop icon; we keep the button we get back, since we need it when the window closes
    63		window.close_requested.connect(_on_window_close_requested.bind(window, button))  # Then we put _on_window_close_requested on this window's "I want to close" list, along with the window and its taskbar button, so when it closes we know which two to delete
    64		_update_active_button()  # Finally we check again which window is on top: the new window was just placed last, so its button turns dark and the previous one goes back to normal
    65	
    66	
    67	## Before opening any new window, we call this first to ask: may we open another one?
    68	## The number of children in the window layer is the number of open windows (minimised ones count too; they are only hidden). Later, other software and opened files will also ask it first.
    69	func _can_open_window() -> bool:
    70		return _window_layer.get_child_count() < MAX_OPEN_WINDOWS  # If fewer than 15 windows are open, we answer "yes"; at 15 we answer "no"
    71	
    72	
    73	## Each time we open a window, we call this: we put a new button in the taskbar's button row, with the software's name on it.
    74	## The button remembers which window it belongs to, and when the player clicks it we show that window. The finished button is handed back to the caller, to be deleted together with the window when it closes.
    75	func _add_taskbar_button(name_key: String, window: Control) -> Button:
    76		var button := Button.new()  # First we build a new button; it is not in the scene tree yet, so the player cannot see it
    77		button.text = name_key  # We write the translation key of the software's name on the button; when shown, the button looks it up in ui_text.csv by itself and turns it into "This PC"
    78		button.pressed.connect(_on_taskbar_button_pressed.bind(window))  # We put our _on_taskbar_button_pressed on this button's "I was clicked" list, along with its window, so when we are called we know which one to show
    79		_taskbar_buttons.add_child(button)  # Then we put it in the taskbar's button row; the row places it to the right of the existing buttons
    80		_taskbar_button_of[window] = button  # Then we record "this window's button is this one"; we need it to find the button from the window when painting colours
    81		return button  # Finally we hand the button back; _on_this_pc_icon_activated() binds it together with the window to "I want to close"
    82	
    83	
    84	## Whenever the window order or which windows are shown/hidden changes, we call this: we find the window now on top, paint its taskbar button dark, and put the other buttons back to normal.
    85	## Called from five places: opening a window, clicking a taskbar button, minimising, show desktop, and closing a window.
    86	func _update_active_button() -> void:
    87		var active_window: Control = null  # First we assume no window is in use (for example, all are minimised)
    88		for window in _window_layer.get_children():  # We look at the windows one by one, from the bottom up
    89			if window.visible and not window.is_queued_for_deletion():  # If this window is visible and is not about to be deleted
    90				active_window = window  # we take it as the top one for now; later ones are drawn higher, so the one left after we finish is the real top window
    91		for window in _taskbar_button_of:  # Then we take out each open window and its button, one by one
    92			var button := _taskbar_button_of[window]  # We find this window's taskbar button
    93			if window == active_window:  # If it is the window in use
    94				button.add_theme_stylebox_override("normal", _active_button_style)  # we swap the button's normal background for the dark one
    95			else:  # Otherwise
    96				button.remove_theme_stylebox_override("normal")  # we take off the swapped-in background, and the button goes back to Godot's default look
    97	
    98	
    99	## Called when the player clicks one of the taskbar buttons (the button emits pressed): we show the window that belongs to this button and bring it in front of all the others.
   100	func _on_taskbar_button_pressed(window: Control) -> void:
   101		window.show()  # First we show the window; if it was minimised (hidden) before, it is visible again now
   102		_window_layer.move_child(window, -1)  # Then we move it to the last place in the window layer; later children are drawn on top, so it covers the other windows
   103		_update_active_button()  # Finally we repaint the colours: its button turns dark and the previous top one goes back to normal
   104	
   105	
   106	## Called when the player clicks a window's — button (that window emits minimize_requested): we hide that window.
   107	## The window is only out of sight, not deleted, and everything in it is still there; later, when its taskbar button is clicked, we show it again.
   108	func _on_window_minimize_requested(window: Control) -> void:
   109		window.hide()  # We hide the window that sent the request, and the desktop (or another window) behind it shows through
   110		_update_active_button()  # Then we repaint the colours: the next window that shows through becomes the one in use; if only the desktop is left behind, no button turns dark
   111	
   112	
   113	## Called when the player clicks the "Show desktop" button at the far right of the taskbar (the button emits pressed): we minimise every window to reveal the desktop (GDD 5.2).
   114	## The windows are only hidden, and their taskbar buttons are all still there; whichever button is clicked, that window comes back.
   115	func _on_show_desktop_button_pressed() -> void:
   116		for window in _window_layer.get_children():  # We take the windows out of the window layer one by one
   117			window.hide()  # and hide each one, the same as the player clicking its own —
   118		_update_active_button()  # Finally we repaint the colours: now no window is in use, so every button goes back to normal
   119	
   120	
   121	## Called when the player clicks a window's × button (that window emits close_requested): we delete that window together with its taskbar button.
   122	## Unlike minimising, once closed the window is gone; to see it again, a new one has to be opened from the desktop icon.
   123	func _on_window_close_requested(window: Control, button: Button) -> void:
   124		_taskbar_button_of.erase(window)  # First we cross this window out of the "which button belongs to which window" record, so colour painting no longer cares about it
   125		button.queue_free()  # Then we delete this button on the taskbar; the button row moves the buttons on its right to the left by itself to fill the gap
   126		window.queue_free()  # Then we delete the window itself; the window (or desktop) behind it shows through
   127		_update_active_button()  # Finally we repaint the colours: the window that shows through becomes the one in use
